lessons.title: Cereal Grains: Corn, Wheat, Barley, Sorghum, and By-Products
lessons.body: Cereal grains are the backbone of pig diets, providing 60-80% of the energy in most African pig feeds. Maize (corn) is the gold standard, with about 3,350 kcal digestible energy (DE) per kg and 8-9% crude protein. In East and Southern Africa, white maize is common, but yellow maize is better because it contains beta-carotene. When maize is expensive, wheat (3,300 kcal DE/kg) can replace it, but wheat tends to be sticky when ground fine; use a coarser grind. Barley (3,000 kcal DE/kg) is lower in energy due to fiber, so limit to 20-30% of the diet for growing pigs. Sorghum (3,200 kcal DE/kg) grows well in dry areas like Sudan and Nigeria. Use low-tannin varieties; high-tannin sorghum reduces protein digestibility and palatability. By-products like maize bran (2,200 kcal DE/kg) and wheat bran (2,000 kcal DE/kg) are cheaper but high in fiber, so keep them under 15% for young pigs and up to 30% for sows. Always grind grains to a medium texture (700-800 microns) for best digestion. Store grains dry (below 12% moisture) to prevent aflatoxin, especially in humid regions. A simple on-farm test: squeeze a handful of grain; if it clumps, it's too wet. For small-scale farmers, mixing maize with 10% cassava chip meal can stretch energy without hurting performance. Remember, energy is the most expensive nutrient, so choose the cheapest energy source per kcal. In Kenya, a 50 kg bag of maize may cost KES 2,500, while wheat bran is KES 1,200; calculate cost per kg of DE to decide. Always introduce new grains gradually over 5-7 days to avoid digestive upset.

lessons.title: Fats and Oils: Sources, Quality, and Inclusion Levels
lessons.body: Fats and oils are concentrated energy sources, providing 2.25 times more energy than carbohydratesâabout 8,500 kcal DE/kg for most feed-grade fats. In pig diets, they improve palatability, reduce dust, and increase energy density for fast-growing pigs. Common sources in Africa include vegetable oils (palm, soybean, sunflower, groundnut), animal fats (tallow, lard), and by-products like restaurant grease. Palm oil is widely available in West and Central Africa; it is high in saturated fat, making it solid at room temperature but stable. Soybean oil is rich in polyunsaturated fats but prone to rancidity. Quality matters: rancid fats smell like paint or crayons, cause diarrhea, and destroy vitamins. Always smell and taste a sample before buying. For inclusion levels, start with 2-3% for weaner pigs (5-15 kg), 3-5% for growing pigs (15-50 kg), and up to 5-8% for lactating sows. Too much fat (above 8%) can cause soft pork and reduce feed intake. When adding fat, increase vitamin E and selenium to prevent oxidative damage. Mix fat thoroughly with the feed; if using solid fat, melt it first and spray onto the mash. In hot climates, store fats in a cool, dark place and use within 4-6 weeks. A practical trick: mix 1 kg of fat with 10 kg of ground maize to make a pre-mix, then blend into the full batch. For smallholders, 1 litre of palm oil (about 900 g) can replace 2.5 kg of maize in energy terms, but cost per kg of oil must be less than 2.5 times the cost of maize to be economical. In Uganda, a litre of crude palm oil costs UGX 5,000, while 2.5 kg of maize costs UGX 3,000; so maize is cheaper. Always calculate before buying.

lessons.title: Root and Tuber Crops: Cassava, Sweet Potato, and Their Processing
lessons.body: Root and tuber crops are vital energy sources in tropical Africa, especially where cereals are scarce or expensive. Cassava (manioc) is the most common, with 3,000-3,300 kcal DE/kg on a dry matter basis, but fresh roots contain 60-70% water and only 30-35% starch. Fresh cassava also contains cyanogenic glucosides (linamarin), which release hydrogen cyanide (HCN) when eaten. Processing is essential: peel, wash, and either sun-dry for 2-3 days or soak in water for 24-48 hours, then dry. Dried cassava chips can be ground into meal and included at 20-40% for growing pigs, up to 50% for sows. However, cassava is low in protein (1-2%) and amino acids, so you must add protein sources like soybean meal or fish meal. Sweet potato (3,200 kcal DE/kg dry) is another option; it is less toxic but high in moisture. Dried sweet potato chips can replace 20-30% of maize. Both crops are bulky and low in energy per kg of fresh weight, so drying is key. In Nigeria, a tonne of fresh cassava costs NGN 30,000, but after drying yields only 300 kg of chips; the cost per kg of dry chips becomes NGN 100, which may still be cheaper than maize at NGN 200/kg. Use a simple solar dryer or concrete floor to dry chips quickly to avoid mold. Never feed raw, wet cassava peels to pigsâthey cause scouring. For small-scale farmers, a mix of 30% cassava chip meal, 40% maize, and 30% protein concentrate works well for grower pigs. Always test a small batch first and watch for diarrhea or poor growth. Store dried chips in airtight bags in a dry place.

lessons.title: By-Products from Food and Biofuel Industries
lessons.body: By-products from food and biofuel processing can cut feed costs by 20-40% if used correctly. Common ones in Africa include maize bran, wheat bran, rice bran, brewery waste (spent grain), molasses, and glycerol from biodiesel. Maize bran (2,200 kcal DE/kg) and wheat bran (2,000 kcal DE/kg) are high in fiber, so limit to 10-15% for piglets, 20-30% for growers, and up to 40% for sows. Rice bran is widely available in rice-growing areas like Tanzania and Nigeria; full-fat rice bran has 2,800 kcal DE/kg but goes rancid quickly due to oil, so use within 2 weeks or stabilize by heating. Brewery waste (spent grain) is 70-80% water; it provides 1,500-2,000 kcal DE/kg on a dry basis and 20-25% protein, but must be used fresh (within 2 days) or ensiled. Molasses (2,200 kcal DE/kg) is a cheap energy source but causes loose stools; limit to 5-10% and mix well. Glycerol from biodiesel (3,000 kcal DE/kg) is becoming available; include up to 5% for growing pigs. When using by-products, always adjust the diet for fiber and protein. For example, a diet with 30% wheat bran needs extra soybean meal to meet lysine needs. Also, check for contaminants: aflatoxin in maize bran, salmonella in brewery waste. A practical rule: never use more than two by-products in one diet, and always run a small trial with 5-10 pigs before scaling up. In South Africa, wet brewery waste is often free, but transport costs may limit use to farms within 50 km. Calculate the cost per kg of DE after drying or transport. For smallholders, mixing 20% maize bran, 10% molasses, and 70% home-mixed concentrate can work for sows. Store dry by-products in a dry, ventilated area.

lessons.title: Energy Utilization and Efficiency in Pigs
lessons.body: Pigs don't eat calories; they eat feed, and how efficiently they convert that feed into meat depends on energy utilization. The key measure is feed conversion ratio (FCR): kg of feed per kg of gain. A good FCR for growing pigs is 2.5-3.0; if your FCR is above 3.5, energy is being wasted. Energy is used first for maintenance (body functions, temperature control), then for growth. In hot climates, pigs eat less to avoid heat, so they may not get enough energy. To improve efficiency, match energy density to the pig's needs: young pigs need 3,400 kcal DE/kg, growers 3,200 kcal DE/kg, and sows 3,000 kcal DE/kg. If energy is too low, pigs eat more but may not grow fast; if too high, they eat less and may not get enough protein. The ideal energy-to-protein ratio is about 18-20 kcal DE per gram of crude protein for growers. Grinding feed to 700-800 microns increases digestibility by 5-10%. Pelleting further improves FCR by 5-8% but is costly for smallholders. Adding fat increases energy density and reduces feed intake, so adjust protein upward. Water is critical: pigs need 2-3 litres of water per kg of feed, and restricted water reduces energy utilization. Health status matters: worms, coccidia, and respiratory disease divert energy to immune response. Deworm every 3 months. Also, avoid overfeeding: a 50 kg pig needs about 2 kg of feed per day (6,400 kcal DE) for 700 g gain. Weigh feed and pigs regularly to calculate FCR. In Uganda, a farmer who improved FCR from 3.5 to 2.8 saved 20% on feed costs. Simple records: date, pig weight, feed offered, feed refused. Use a hanging scale and a 20 kg bucket. If FCR worsens, check feed quality, health, and temperature. Energy efficiency is the cheapest way to increase profit.

lessons.title: Formulating Diets to Meet Energy Specifications
lessons.body: Formulating a pig diet to meet energy specifications means balancing energy with other nutrients at the lowest cost. Start by knowing the energy requirement of your pigs: weaners (5-15 kg) need 3,400 kcal DE/kg, growers (15-50 kg) 3,200 kcal DE/kg, finishers (50-100 kg) 3,100 kcal DE/kg, gestating sows 3,000 kcal DE/kg, and lactating sows 3,300 kcal DE/kg. Next, list available energy sources with their DE values and costs. For example, maize (3,350 kcal/kg, $0.30/kg), cassava chips (3,100 kcal/kg, $0.20/kg), wheat bran (2,000 kcal/kg, $0.15/kg), and palm oil (8,500 kcal/kg, $1.00/kg). Calculate cost per 1,000 kcal DE: maize = $0.09, cassava = $0.06, wheat bran = $0.075, palm oil = $0.12. So cassava is cheapest per kcal. But you must also meet protein, amino acid, mineral, and vitamin needs. Use a simple spreadsheet or a free app like Feed Formulation (available on Google Play) or Excel Solver. For smallholders, a Pearson's Square method works for two ingredients. Example: mix maize (3,350 kcal) and wheat bran (2,000 kcal) to get 3,000 kcal. Let X = kg maize, Y = kg wheat bran. X + Y = 100. 3350X + 2000Y = 300000. Solve: X = 66.7 kg, Y = 33.3 kg. Then add 20% protein concentrate (e.g., soybean meal + fish meal + minerals). Always include 0.5% salt, 1% calcium, and 0.5% vitamin-mineral premix. Test the mix with 5 pigs for 2 weeks; check feed intake, growth, and manure. If pigs refuse feed, add molasses (2-3%) or reduce fiber. If manure is loose, reduce oil or molasses. Keep records of ingredients, costs, and pig performance. In Kenya, a farmer can formulate a 100 kg grower diet: 60 kg maize, 20 kg cassava chips, 15 kg soybean meal, 3 kg fish meal, 1 kg minerals, 1 kg salt. This gives about 3,200 kcal DE/kg and 18% protein. Adjust based on local prices. Always weigh ingredients accurately; a 10% error in energy can cost 15% in growth.

quiz.q: Which cereal grain is considered the gold standard for energy in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Maize provides about 3,350 kcal DE/kg and is highly digestible, making it the preferred energy source.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with high-tannin sorghum in pig feed?
options: A) It is too high in energy
B) It reduces protein digestibility and palatability
D) It is toxic to pigs
quiz.explanation: Tannins bind proteins and reduce feed intake, so low-tannin varieties are recommended.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum inclusion of wheat bran for young pigs?
quiz.explanation: Wheat bran is high in fiber, so it should be limited to 15% for piglets to avoid digestive upset.

quiz.q: How much energy does feed-grade fat provide compared to carbohydrates?
quiz.explanation: Fats provide about 8,500 kcal DE/kg, which is 2.25 times the energy of carbohydrates.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of rancid fat?
quiz.explanation: Rancid fats develop off-odors due to oxidation, which can harm pig health.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended inclusion of fat for lactating sows?
quiz.explanation: Up to 8% fat can be used for lactating sows to increase energy density without causing soft pork.

quiz.q: Why must cassava be processed before feeding to pigs?
quiz.explanation: Cassava contains linamarin, which releases hydrogen cyanide; processing like drying or soaking removes it.

quiz.q: What is the recommended inclusion level of dried cassava chips for growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: Dried cassava can replace 20-40% of maize in grower diets if protein is supplemented.

quiz.q: Which root crop is less toxic but high in moisture?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato has lower toxin levels but must be dried to concentrate energy.

quiz.q: What is a key step when using fresh cassava peels?
quiz.explanation: Drying reduces moisture and cyanide content, making peels safe for pigs.

quiz.q: Which by-product is high in fiber and should be limited to 10-15% for piglets?
quiz.explanation: Maize bran has about 2,200 kcal DE/kg but high fiber, so it can cause digestive issues in young pigs.

quiz.q: Why should full-fat rice bran be used within 2 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Rice bran contains oil that oxidizes rapidly, leading to rancidity and reduced palatability.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended inclusion of molasses in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Molasses is a cheap energy source but causes loose stools if over 10%.

quiz.q: Which by-product from biodiesel production can be used as an energy source?
quiz.explanation: Glycerol is a by-product of biodiesel and provides about 3,000 kcal DE/kg for pigs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum inclusion of glycerol for growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: Up to 5% glycerol can be used without affecting performance or carcass quality.

quiz.q: What does FCR stand for in pig production?
quiz.explanation: FCR is the kg of feed required per kg of body weight gain, a key measure of efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a good FCR for growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: An FCR of 2.5-3.0 indicates efficient feed conversion; above 3.5 is wasteful.

quiz.q: How does hot climate affect energy utilization in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Heat stress reduces feed intake, so pigs may not meet their energy needs.

quiz.q: What is the ideal energy-to-protein ratio for growing pigs?
options: A) 10-12 kcal DE per g CP
B) 18-20 kcal DE per g CP
C) 25-30 kcal DE per g CP
D) 35-40 kcal DE per g CP
quiz.explanation: This ratio ensures pigs get enough protein relative to energy for optimal growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended particle size for ground pig feed?
quiz.explanation: A medium grind of 700-800 microns improves digestibility without causing ulcers.

quiz.q: How much water does a pig need per kg of feed?
quiz.explanation: Adequate water is essential for digestion and nutrient utilization; 2-3 litres per kg feed is typical.

quiz.q: What is the energy requirement for weaner pigs (5-15 kg)?
quiz.explanation: Weaners need highly digestible, energy-dense diets to support rapid growth.

quiz.q: Which method can be used to formulate a diet with two energy sources?
quiz.explanation: Pearson's Square is simple for two ingredients, while linear programming (e.g., Excel Solver) handles multiple nutrients.

quiz.q: In the example, what is the cost per 1,000 kcal DE for maize at $0.30/kg?
quiz.explanation: Maize provides 3,350 kcal/kg, so $0.30 / 3.35 = $0.09 per 1,000 kcal.

quiz.q: What is a key mineral that must be added to all pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Salt (sodium chloride) is essential for electrolyte balance and is typically added at 0.5%.

quiz.q: Why should you test a new feed mix on a small group of pigs first?
options: B) To avoid wasting feed on a bad batch
C) To see if pigs like it
quiz.explanation: A small trial helps identify palatability, digestive issues, or performance problems before scaling up.

quiz.q: What is the energy content of palm oil per kg?
quiz.explanation: Palm oil, like other fats, provides about 8,500 kcal DE/kg, making it a concentrated energy source.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of poor feed conversion?
quiz.explanation: An FCR above 3.5 indicates inefficiency, often due to poor feed quality, health, or environment.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using by-products in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: By-products are often cheaper per kg of energy, reducing overall feed costs.

quiz.q: What should you do if pigs refuse a new feed mix?
options: B) Add molasses or reduce fiber
quiz.explanation: Adding palatable ingredients like molasses or reducing high-fiber components can improve acceptance.
